pages.text: Senam sat on her grandfather’s wooden stool. “Nana, is this stool alive?” she asked. Nana Dapaah smiled. “Let us find out. Living things do special things. Let us look at a tree, a stone and the stool.”
sentences: Senam sat on her grandfather’s wooden stool.
“Nana, is this stool alive?” she asked.
Nana Dapaah smiled.
“Let us find out.
Living things do special things.
Let us look at a tree, a stone and the stool.”
pages.alt: In a sunlit Ghanaian compound courtyard, Senam sits on a carved wooden stool beside smiling Nana Dapaah near a leafy mango tree and a smooth grey stone.

pages.text: First, they looked at the mango tree. It grew taller each year. It needed water and air. Its leaves moved towards the light. It also made seeds to grow new trees. “The tree is alive,” said Senam.
sentences: First, they looked at the mango tree.
It grew taller each year.
It needed water and air.
Its leaves moved towards the light.
It also made seeds to grow new trees.
“The tree is alive,” said Senam.
pages.alt: Senam touching the bark of a tall leafy mango tree hung with ripe mangoes while Nana Dapaah stands beside her pointing gently up at the sunlit leaves.

pages.text: Next, they looked at a stone. It did not grow. It did not need food, water or air. It did not make babies. “The stone is not alive,” said Senam. “It was never alive,” said Nana Dapaah.
sentences: Next, they looked at a stone.
It did not grow.
It did not need food, water or air.
It did not make babies.
“The stone is not alive,” said Senam.
“It was never alive,” said Nana Dapaah.
pages.alt: Senam crouching in the courtyard holding a smooth grey river stone in both hands while Nana Dapaah leans on his walking stick and nods kindly.

pages.text: Then Senam studied the stool. It did not grow, eat or breathe. “It is not alive now,” said Nana. “But it was once part of a tree. So we say the stool is made from something that was once alive.”
sentences: Then Senam studied the stool.
It did not grow, eat or breathe.
“It is not alive now,” said Nana.
“But it was once part of a tree.
So we say the stool is made from something that was once alive.”
pages.alt: Nana Dapaah kneeling beside the traditional carved wooden stool and pointing to the curved wood grain on its seat while Senam leans close to look.

pages.text: Nana Dapaah made three groups. “Living things grow, need food and air, and make young ones. Things that were never alive, like stones and sand, do none of these. Things that were once alive, like wood, paper and leather, used to be living things.”
sentences: Nana Dapaah made three groups.
“Living things grow, need food and air, and make young ones.
Things that were never alive, like stones and sand, do none of these.
Things that were once alive, like wood, paper and leather, used to be living things.”
pages.alt: On a woven courtyard mat, Nana Dapaah and Senam arrange three neat groups of objects: a potted green seedling, smooth stones, and the carved wooden stool with a woven basket.

pages.text: Senam drew the three groups on a picture chart and added three more items to each. At school the next day, she showed her teacher. “Now I can tell the difference,” she said. “And I will not break a branch from a living tree without a reason.”
sentences: Senam drew the three groups on a picture chart and added three more items to each.
At school the next day, she showed her teacher.
“Now I can tell the difference,” she said.
“And I will not break a branch from a living tree without a reason.”
pages.alt: In a bright Ghanaian classroom, Senam proudly holds up a colourful picture-only poster showing drawings of trees, stones and wooden stools to her smiling teacher.

activities.question: Why is the stone not alive?
options: It does not grow, eat or make young ones

activities.question: What do we say about the wooden stool?
options: It is made from something once alive

activities.definition: Alive: able to grow, need food and air, and make young ones.
